title: Functions
description: Defining functions with def, parameters, and return values

exercises.title: Defining a Function
exercises.content: A function is a reusable block of code with a name. You define it with the 'def' keyword, then call it by writing its name with parentheses (). The code inside the function doesn't run until you call it!
exercises.code:
def say_hello():
    print("Hello!")
    print("Nice to meet you!")

say_hello()
say_hello()

highlights.note: 'def' defines a function. The name is 'say_hello'. The parentheses and colon are required.
The indented lines are the function body. They only run when the function is called.
Calling the function twice runs the body twice — 4 lines of output from 2 lines of code!

exercises.title: Parameters
exercises.content: Functions can accept inputs called parameters. You put the parameter name inside the parentheses when defining the function. When you call the function, you pass in a value — that value gets assigned to the parameter name inside the function.
exercises.code:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

greet("Alice")
greet("Bob")

highlights.note: 'name' is a parameter — a placeholder for whatever value gets passed in.
Calling greet("Alice") makes name = "Alice" inside the function.
Calling greet("Bob") makes name = "Bob" — same function, different input!

exercises.title: Return Values
exercises.content: A function can send a value back to the caller using 'return'. This is different from print — print shows text on screen, but return sends a value back that can be stored in a variable or used in an expression. Once return runs, the function immediately stops.
exercises.code:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)
print(double(3) + 1)

highlights.note: 'return' sends x * 2 back to the caller. It does NOT print anything!
double(5) returns 10, which gets stored in 'result'.
You can use the return value directly — double(3) returns 6, then 6 + 1 = 7.

exercises.title: Functions with Conditionals
exercises.content: Functions become really powerful when you combine them with if statements. A function can make decisions and return different values depending on its input. This lets you package up logic and reuse it.

highlights.note: If age is 18 or more, return "adult" and stop.
Otherwise, return "minor". Only one return ever runs — the function stops at the first one it hits.
